title: Australian sharemarket ends flat as technology plummets and oil falls amid US-Iran peace talks
text:

It was a mixed day for the Australian sharemarket on Monday, which ended the day relatively flat, amid negotiations to end the US war against Iran.

The ASX 200 was down 12.6 points, or 0.1 per cent, to 8816.1, while the broader All Ordinaries fell 16.1 points, or 0.2 per cent, to 9031.2.

Six of the 11 sectors finished in the red on Monday — led by technology, health care, communication services and energy.

The Australian dollar is now buying 70 US cents.

Brent crude plunged below $US80 per barrel after the US and Iran agreed to create a “de-confliction cell” to stop fighting in Lebanon. Further peace talks are expected this week.

Major miners suffered, with PLS diving 5.95 per cent, BHP dipping 1.73 per cent and Fortescue down 0.76 per cent.

Meanwhile, Woodside Energy fell 0.9 per cent and Karoon Energy slid 3.13 per cent.

Gold producers fared better, with Evolution Mining soaring 3.35 cent, Genesis Minerals jumping 3.36 per cent and Northern Star spiking 1.58 per cent.

Technology was the weakest sector, with WiseTech Global plummeting 18.44 per cent after the Australian Federal Police began investigating executive chairman Richard White over claims he exploited a woman’s immigration status and financial insecurity.

Xero fell 4.54 per cent and TechnologyOne dipped 0.4 per cent.

Despite mining and tech sectors falling, the financial and consumer discretionary sector offset those weaknesses to balance out the ASX.

Among the big four banks, Commonwealth Bank rose 0.62 per cent, ANZ climbed 0.63 per cent, NAB inched up 0.34 per cent and Westpac was up 0.31 per cent.

Insurers QBE and Insurance Australia Group were also up 1.54 per cent and 3.01 per cent respectively.

In company news, Inghams sank 4.76 per cent after a full lockdown across its WA farms and processing sites following the detection of H5N1 avian influenza in two wild birds at Esperance.

Stokes family company SGH leapt three per cent as it announced a share buyback of up to $500m.

The a2 Milk Company also jumped 0.89 per cent after announcing a $300m special dividend following Chinese approval to transfer two baby formula registrations to its own brand.

EQT Holdings descended 11.56 per cent after the parent company of Equity Trustees announced plans to wind up its $95bn independent superannuation trusteeship services.

Humm Group was the worst performer, diving 22.22 per cent.

Looking ahead, the Aussie dollar will be driven by Wednesday’s May CPI report and Thursday’s labour force report.

From the US perspective, further updates from peace talks and Thursday night’s core PCE inflation data will be key influences.

“The read-through here is a hotter inflation print combined with a solid rebound in jobs would undoubtedly keep the door wide open for further RBA rate hikes before year end,” IG Markets senior analyst Tony Sycamore said.

“Conversely, cooler readings across both releases would add serious weight to the view that the RBA’s current policy setting is restrictive enough.

“The interest rate market starts this week pricing in six basis points of rate hikes for the RBA’s August meeting, with a cumulative 15 basis points of RBA rate hikes priced for the remainder of 2026.”
